steps.title: Frame the Trade-off
steps.description: The agent must maximize resolution rate across five prompt variants without wasting too many tickets on weak arms.

steps.title: Survey the Arms
steps.description: Each arm carries its running statistics: pull count and estimated mean reward, from Arm C at 0.87 to Arm E at 0.49.

steps.title: Apply a Selection Strategy
steps.description: Epsilon-greedy explores 10% of the time, UCB1 adds an optimism bonus for rarely-pulled arms, and Thompson sampling draws from each arm's Beta posterior.

steps.title: Pull the Chosen Arm
steps.description: The strategy picks one variant, which is served to the next incoming support ticket.

steps.title: Observe the Reward
steps.description: The ticket either resolves (+1) or escalates (0), giving a single binary reward for this round.

steps.title: Track Regret and Update Posteriors
steps.description: Cumulative regret against the optimal arm holds at 3.2%, and the pulled arm's Beta posterior updates with the observed outcome.

steps.title: Loop to the Next Round
steps.description: Updated posteriors feed back to the agent, which shifts more pulls toward the strongest arms over time.

steps.title: Converge on the Winner
steps.description: After enough rounds the agent settles on Arm C at 87% resolution, a 23% lift over the baseline prompt.

name: Evolutionary Discovery Algorithms(EDA)
description: Bio-inspired optimization that evolves solutions through selection, mutation, and crossover

tldr.what: Maintains a population of candidate solutions, applies selection and genetic operators (mutation, crossover) to evolve better solutions across generations.
tldr.when: Large search spaces where you need multiple diverse solutions or must balance competing objectives without a clear analytical path.
tldr.watchOut: Convergence to local optima is common; fitness evaluation cost scales with population size and generations, making it expensive for slow-to-evaluate domains.

flow.title: Evolutionary Discovery Algorithms
flow.description: A population of 50 agent-prompt variants evolves across generations. Each variant is scored on task success, the fittest are selected, then crossover and mutation breed the next generation while a diversity monitor keeps the population from collapsing.

Evolve best agent prompt
Fitness = success rate - 0.1×length

Generation 1 / 100

[terse, no examples]
fitness: 0.45

🟢 Variant B
[CoT, 2 examples]
fitness: 0.73

🔵 Variant C
[role + rubric]
fitness: 0.68

⚖️ Fitness Evaluation
Run each variant on task suite
score = accuracy - length penalty

💀 Weak Variant
fitness 0.12
culled from pool

🏅 Selection
Tournament k=3
top 30% reproduce

👑 Elitism
Keep top 5 unchanged

🔀 Crossover
Uniform, p=0.8
blend two parent prompts

✨ Mutation
p=0.1
tweak instruction / example

📊 Diversity Monitor
Guard against collapse
inject fresh mutations

🐣 Offspring
Generation n+1
best fitness: 0.94

🏆 Evolved Agent
Gen 100, 97% success
60% shorter prompt

steps.title: Seed the Population
steps.description: Fifty randomly-composed prompt variants form Generation 1, each a different mix of instructions, examples, and role framing.

steps.title: Sample Individuals
steps.description: Representative variants span the fitness landscape, from a terse Variant A at 0.45 to a chain-of-thought Variant B at 0.73.

steps.title: Evaluate Fitness
steps.description: Every variant runs against the task suite; fitness is accuracy minus a length penalty, so bloated prompts are punished.

steps.title: Select Parents
steps.description: Tournament selection with k=3 lets the top 30% reproduce, while elitism copies the best 5 straight into the next generation.

steps.title: Crossover
steps.description: Uniform crossover at p=0.8 blends two parent prompts, mixing one parent's instructions with the other's examples.

steps.title: Mutate and Guard Diversity
steps.description: Mutation at p=0.1 tweaks an instruction or example, and the diversity monitor injects fresh variation if the population is converging too fast.

steps.title: Form the Next Generation
steps.description: Elites, crossover children, and mutants combine into the offspring generation, best fitness now 0.94, which loops back as the new population.

steps.title: Converge on the Evolved Agent
steps.description: After 100 generations the population yields a prompt hitting 97% success with a 60% shorter prompt than the hand-written baseline.

name: Multi-Criteria Weighted Scoring(MCWS)
description: Systematic prioritization using weighted scoring across multiple evaluation criteria

tldr.what: Scores candidates against multiple weighted criteria, then ranks by total score to surface trade-offs and justify decisions.
tldr.when: Choosing between competing options where different stakeholders care about different factors and transparency matters.
tldr.watchOut: Weights and scoring scales are subjective; small changes can flip rankings, masking that the real disagreement is about values.

flow.title: Multi-Criteria Weighted Scoring

name: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis(MCDA)

tldr.what: Scores alternatives against weighted criteria using pairwise comparisons and consistency checks to rank complex multi-stakeholder decisions.
tldr.when: Choosing between 3+ options with conflicting priorities, multiple stakeholders, and criteria that cannot be reduced to a single metric.
tldr.watchOut: Weights and scores are subjective; small changes in criteria weighting can reverse the final ranking, masking the real decision driver.

steps.title: Frame the Decision

steps.title: Commit the Selection

name: Dynamic Priority Queue Systems(DPQS)
description: Intelligent queue management with dynamic priority adjustment based on changing conditions

tldr.what: Adjusts task priority in real-time using formulas that combine urgency, user tier, wait time, and resource cost, reordering queue dynamically.
tldr.when: Many competing tasks with different deadlines and resource costs where static priority fails and fairness across user groups matters.
tldr.watchOut: Priority inversions and starvation occur when aging bonuses or formulas don't prevent low-priority tasks from blocking high-value work indefinitely.

flow.title: Dynamic Priority Queue Systems

tldr.when: Systems serving personalized feeds or recommendations to many users where engagement, diversity, and freshness matter simultaneously.
tldr.watchOut: Feedback loops can amplify biases: users click what they see, ranking promotes what gets clicked, narrowing diversity over time.

name: Agent Payment Mandates (AP2)(AP2)
description: Authorizes agent-initiated purchases through a chain of cryptographically signed, verifiable-credential mandates instead of handing an agent raw card details. An Intent Mandate captures the user's up-front constraints (max price, allowed merchants, time-to-live) so the agent can buy while the user is not present; a Cart Mandate is merchant-signed and user-co-signed for the exact items and price, giving what-you-see-is-what-you-pay; and a Payment Mandate is shared with the payment network. The signed chain forms a non-repudiable audit trail that resolves authorization, authenticity, and accountability for autonomous spend, and it is rail-agnostic with an A2A-x402 profile for crypto rails. Distinct from authenticated-delegation: that pattern grants an agent scoped authority to act, whereas AP2 binds each specific purchase to a signed mandate chain a payment network can independently verify.
features: Intent Mandate encodes user constraints (max price, allowed merchants, TTL) for human-not-present purchases
Cart Mandate is merchant-signed and user-co-signed for exact items and price
Payment Mandate is shared with the payment network to authorize settlement
Chained verifiable credentials form a non-repudiable audit trail
Resolves authorization, authenticity, and accountability for autonomous spend
Rail-agnostic, with an A2A-x402 extension for stablecoin settlement

tldr.what: Agent requests purchases within user-signed constraints; merchant and user co-sign exact cart; payment network verifies the signed mandate chain before settling.
tldr.when: Autonomous agent spending where user cannot approve each transaction in real time, and audit trail and non-repudiation matter more than speed.
tldr.watchOut: Mandate expiry, revocation, and constraint drift create gaps; if agent or merchant signs outside user intent, the chain breaks and disputes become costly.

steps.description: The user delegates a bounded purchase without being present, expressed as constraints rather than a blank check.

steps.title: Intent Mandate Signed
steps.description: Constraints (max price, destination, TTL) are signed up front into a verifiable credential the agent carries as proof of authority.

steps.title: Agent Shops, Merchant Signs the Cart
steps.description: The agent finds a fare and the airline returns a merchant-signed Cart Mandate for the exact items and price.

steps.title: User Co-Signs the Cart Mandate
steps.description: The user (or the user's device) co-signs, locking what-you-see-is-what-you-pay, then a Payment Mandate is prepared for the network.

steps.title: Network Verifies the Mandate Chain
steps.description: The payment network checks that the Intent, Cart, and Payment signatures line up and the constraint check passes, without seeing the raw card.

steps.title: Over-Cap Upsell Rejected
steps.description: An upsell that would push the total to $832 exceeds the $800 Intent Mandate cap, so no valid Cart Mandate can be signed and the charge is refused.

steps.title: Settlement and Audit Trail
steps.description: The in-budget fare settles at $712 and every step is recorded as a signed credential, giving a non-repudiable trail for dispute resolution.

name: Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP)(ACP)
description: Open standard co-developed by Stripe and OpenAI (Apache-2.0, September 2025) for completing a purchase against a merchant that stays the merchant of record. The merchant exposes agent-facing REST or MCP endpoints (create, update, complete, and cancel checkout) over a product feed; the agent pays with a Stripe-issued Shared Payment Token scoped to a single merchant and cart total, so the agent never sees the buyer's card credentials. It launched as the standard behind ChatGPT Instant Checkout with Etsy sellers and Shopify merchants. Distinct from `model-context-protocol`: MCP is a general tool-calling transport, whereas ACP is a specific checkout contract that can ride over MCP or plain REST.
features: Merchant stays merchant of record and keeps fulfillment and support
Agent-facing REST or MCP endpoints: create, update, complete, cancel checkout
Product feed lets the agent browse the catalog and build a cart before payment
Shared Payment Token scoped to one merchant and one cart total
Agent never sees raw card credentials, so PCI scope stays with the processor
Apache-2.0 open standard; roughly one line of code for existing Stripe merchants

tldr.what: Agent browses merchant product feed, builds cart via REST/MCP endpoints, completes purchase with Stripe-scoped token that never exposes buyer credentials.
tldr.when: Autonomous shopping where an agent must complete transactions while merchant retains fulfillment, support, and merchant-of-record status.
tldr.watchOut: Agents may over-commit to purchases before user confirmation, or fail gracefully if cart totals shift between create and complete calls.

flow.title: Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP)
flow.description: Stripe and OpenAI open standard for an agent to complete a purchase against a merchant that stays the merchant of record. The agent browses a product feed, drives Create / Update / Complete Checkout endpoints, and pays with a Shared Payment Token scoped to one merchant and cart total, so it never sees the card credentials.

steps.description: The buyer gives ChatGPT a natural-language shopping goal with a budget, delegating the whole purchase to the agent.

steps.title: Agent Browses the Merchant Feed
steps.description: The agent reads the merchant product feed, filters to in-stock black running shoes at or below $120, and selects a $98 pair.

steps.title: Create Checkout Returns Totals
steps.description: The agent calls the merchant Create Checkout endpoint; the merchant returns a session with subtotal, shipping, and tax adding up to $112.86, which the agent shows the user.

steps.title: User Approves and the SPT Is Scoped
steps.description: The user confirms, so a Shared Payment Token is issued scoped to this one merchant and the exact $112.86 total, and it cannot be replayed elsewhere or for a larger amount.

steps.title: Complete Checkout With the Scoped Token
steps.description: The agent calls Complete Checkout, sending the token instead of any card credentials. The merchant of record receives it to finalize the order.

steps.title: Merchant Charges via Its Own Stripe
steps.description: The merchant charges the buyer $112.86 through its own Stripe account, keeps PCI scope with the processor, and marks the order paid.

steps.title: Merchant Fulfills and Streams Webhooks
steps.description: The merchant ships the order and emits confirmed, shipped, and delivered webhooks, exactly as it does for any other channel.

steps.title: Purchase Complete, Tracking in Chat
steps.description: The order and tracking surface back in the chat. The purchase completed in-conversation, the agent never touched the card number, and the merchant stayed merchant of record.

name: HTTP-Native Micropayments (x402)(x402)
description: An open payment standard created by Coinbase in 2025 and now stewarded by the x402 Foundation under the Linux Foundation that revives the dormant HTTP 402 Payment Required status as a pay-per-request rail. A server replies 402 with machine-readable payment requirements; the client (human or agent) returns a signed stablecoin payment in an HTTP header; a facilitator verifies the payload and settles the transfer on-chain (EVM chains, Solana, and more), all inside a single request with no accounts, sessions, or API keys. It is a native rail for keyless, sub-cent agent-to-service micropayments and metered tool or data access, and is the crypto profile referenced by the AP2 A2A-x402 extension. Distinct from `agentic-commerce-protocol`: ACP is card-based retail checkout through a merchant of record, whereas x402 is a per-call machine payment settled on-chain.
features: Reuses the HTTP 402 Payment Required status for in-band payment
Server returns machine-readable payment requirements in the 402 response
Client returns a signed stablecoin payment in a request header, then retries
Facilitator verifies the payload and settles the transfer on-chain
Keyless and sessionless: no accounts, API keys, or pre-registration
Enables sub-cent metered access to paid APIs, tools, and data

tldr.what: Server replies 402 with payment terms; client signs a stablecoin transfer in a header and retries; facilitator verifies and settles on-chain in one round trip.
tldr.when: Agents need keyless, per-call access to paid APIs or data without accounts, API keys, or pre-registration.
tldr.watchOut: Signature verification and on-chain settlement latency can cause timeouts if the facilitator is slow or unreliable.

flow.title: HTTP-Native Micropayments (x402)
flow.description: Coinbase x402 revives the HTTP 402 Payment Required status as a pay-per-request rail. A paid API replies 402 with payment requirements, the agent returns a signed stablecoin payment in a header, a facilitator verifies and settles the transfer on-chain, and the same endpoint returns the data, all in-band with no accounts or API keys.

USDC balance

✍️ Agent Signs Payment
0.001 USDC transfer,
keyless, no signup

X-PAYMENT: signed payload

🔎 Facilitator
Verifies the payload

⛓️ Base Network
Settles 0.001 USDC transfer

steps.title: Agent Requests a Paid Quote
steps.description: The agent needs one market-data lookup and sends a plain GET to the x402-gated endpoint with no payment and no account.

steps.title: Server Demands Payment (402)
steps.description: Instead of a 200, the server returns HTTP 402 with machine-readable requirements: pay 0.001 USDC on Base to a given address for this resource.

steps.title: Agent Signs a Stablecoin Payment
steps.description: The agent reads the requirements, draws on its wallet balance, and signs a 0.001 USDC transfer. No API key, invoice, or pre-registration is involved.

steps.title: Retry With the Signed Payment Header
steps.description: The agent re-sends the same request, now carrying the signed payment in the X-PAYMENT header, which reaches the facilitator for verification.

steps.title: Facilitator Verifies and Settles On-Chain
steps.description: The facilitator verifies the signed payload and settles the 0.001 USDC transfer on the Base network.

steps.title: Server Returns the Data
steps.description: With payment settled, the same endpoint returns HTTP 200 with the AAPL quote and a payment-confirmation header.

steps.title: Agent Has the Quote for $0.001
steps.description: The paid call completed in two round trips with no signup, key, or invoice. The agent spent exactly $0.001 and the whole exchange stayed in-band over HTTP.

name: Agent Registry & Discovery(ARD)
description: The discovery layer that lets agents and tool servers find each other at runtime instead of through hard-coded configuration. Three converging mechanisms make this work: A2A Agent Cards, a self-describing JSON manifest served at /.well-known/agent-card.json (RFC 8615) advertising an agent's skills, endpoints, auth schemes, and streaming capabilities; the official MCP Registry (preview September 2025), a federated public catalog and API for publishing and finding MCP servers that is extensible with private enterprise sub-registries; and decentralized naming proposals such as MIT Project NANDA, whose NANDA Index resolves cryptographically verifiable AgentFacts records to endpoints, positioned as DNS for agents. The common pattern is publish a signed capability record, then resolve it by well-known URI or registry query, validate the advertised auth schemes, and bind the agent dynamically. Distinct from `a2a-protocol`: that covers the message transport once a peer is known, while this covers finding and vetting the peer in the first place.
features: Manifests advertise skills, endpoints, auth schemes, and streaming
Federated MCP Registry: public catalog plus private sub-registries
Signed capability records resolved by well-known URI or registry query
Decentralized naming (NANDA Index, verifiable AgentFacts) as DNS for agents
Auth-scheme validation before an agent is wired in dynamically

tldr.what: Agents publish signed capability records at well-known URIs or federated registries, then discover and validate peers dynamically instead of using hard-coded endpoints.
tldr.when: Orchestrators need runtime access to capabilities not built in, or ecosystems where agents and tools join and leave without redeployment.
tldr.watchOut: Registry staleness, compromised signing keys, or auth-scheme mismatches can wire in wrong or malicious agents before validation catches it.

flow.title: Agent Registry & Discovery
flow.description: An orchestrator that needs a capability it was not built with finds a provider at runtime: it queries a registry, resolves the candidate Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json, validates the signature and auth schemes, then binds the agent dynamically instead of hard-coding the integration.

Federated catalog + query API

Decentralized naming, verifiable AgentFacts

📇 Candidate List
3 agents advertise translation

🅰️ translate.example.com
auth: oauth2, transport: HTTPS + SSE

🅱️ cheap-mt.example.net
auth: api-key over plain HTTP

📄 Agent Card
GET /.well-known/agent-card.json (RFC 8615)

⛔ Rejected
No TLS, unsupported auth scheme

🔏 Signature Check
Capability record signed and valid

🔗 Bind Dynamically

steps.title: Capability Gap
steps.description: A Japanese-language ticket arrives; the orchestrator recognizes it lacks a translation skill and needs to find one at runtime.

steps.title: Query the Discovery Layer
steps.description: The orchestrator queries the federated MCP Registry for skill=translation and, in parallel, resolves a human-friendly handle through the NANDA Index.

steps.title: Candidate Resolution
steps.description: Both mechanisms return capability records; the orchestrator assembles a shortlist of three agents that advertise the ja to en translation skill.

steps.title: Resolve the Agent Card
steps.description: For the top candidate it GETs /.well-known/agent-card.json (RFC 8615), reading advertised skills, endpoint, transport, and auth schemes.

steps.title: Validate Trust and Auth
steps.description: It verifies the record signature and confirms an advertised auth scheme matches a credential it holds. The second candidate offers only api-key over plain HTTP and is rejected.

steps.title: Bind Dynamically
steps.description: With signature and auth validated, the orchestrator mints an OAuth token and wires the translation agent into the running task graph with no redeploy.

steps.title: Answer and Cache
steps.description: The translation agent handles the ticket; the resolved card is cached with its ETag so the next lookup skips re-fetching until the card changes.

name: Agent-Readable Web (llms.txt / NLWeb)
description: Supply-side contracts that expose a site's content to agents directly instead of forcing them to scrape rendered HTML. llms.txt (Jeremy Howard, 2024) is a curated Markdown index at /llms.txt plus .md shadow pages that give an LLM high-density, navigation-free content at inference time. Microsoft NLWeb (2025, led by Schema.org co-creator R.V. Guha) goes further with an /ask natural-language endpoint that returns structured JSON grounded in the site's own Schema.org data, with every NLWeb instance doubling as an MCP server. Together they define the agent-readable site, the read-path counterpart to robots.txt for the agentic web.
features: Curated /llms.txt Markdown index of a site
.md shadow pages for clean, high-density content
Structured JSON grounded in Schema.org data
Every NLWeb instance also acts as an MCP server

tldr.what: Site publishes curated Markdown at /llms.txt and .md shadow pages, plus optional /ask endpoint returning structured JSON, so agents retrieve content without scraping HTML.
tldr.when: You operate a service or content site and want agents to access your data reliably, accurately, and at scale without parsing rendered pages.
tldr.watchOut: Requires you to maintain two content surfaces in sync; stale or incomplete /llms.txt defeats the purpose and agents fall back to scraping anyway.

flow.title: Agent-Readable Web (llms.txt / NLWeb)
flow.description: Supply-side content contracts that let an agent read a site directly instead of scraping rendered HTML. The agent checks /llms.txt for a curated Markdown index, pulls clean .md shadow pages, then falls back to a NLWeb /ask endpoint for a structured answer grounded in the site Schema.org data, with the NLWeb instance also usable as an MCP server.

name: Web Bot Auth (Signed Agents)(WBA)
description: An emerging IETF-draft standard (Cloudflare and Google) that lets an agent cryptographically prove its identity to a website using RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures. The agent signs each outbound request with an Ed25519 key, publishes its public keys as a JWKS key directory at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory, and points to it with a Signature-Agent header; the origin fetches the directory, verifies the signature, and decides whether to allow, deny, rate-limit, or price the traffic. It replaces brittle IP-range and User-Agent allowlists, and Cloudflare's Signed Agents productizes it at the edge. Distinct from authenticated-delegation: that proves user-to-agent authority, whereas Web Bot Auth is the inverse, an agent proving its origin to a website.
features: Agent signs each request with RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures (Ed25519)
Public keys published as a JWKS directory at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory
Signature-Agent header points the origin to the key directory
Short expiry windows on signatures limit replay attacks
Origins allow, deny, rate-limit, or price verified agent traffic
Replaces spoofable IP-range and User-Agent allowlists

tldr.what: Agent cryptographically signs each HTTP request with Ed25519, publishes public keys at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory, and origin verifies signature to allow, deny, rate-limit, or price traffic.
tldr.when: Origins need to distinguish legitimate agents from scrapers and grant different access tiers based on verified agent identity rather than spoofable IP ranges or User-Agent headers.
tldr.watchOut: Key rotation and expiry window management become operational burdens; misconfigured signature validation opens doors to replay attacks or signature forgery if not implemented precisely.

flow.title: Web Bot Auth (Signed Agents)
flow.description: An emerging IETF-draft standard (Cloudflare and Google) where an agent signs its HTTP requests per RFC 9421 and publishes keys via a JWKS directory, so origins verify the signature to allow, deny, rate-limit, or price agent traffic instead of trusting spoofable IP or User-Agent allowlists.

steps.title: Agent Signs Its Request
steps.description: A user-directed agent signs each outbound request with an Ed25519 key following RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures.

steps.title: Signed Request Hits the Origin
steps.description: The request arrives carrying Signature-Input, Signature, and a Signature-Agent header pointing to the agent's key directory.

steps.title: Origin Resolves the Key Directory
steps.description: The origin fetches the agent's JWKS directory at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory and looks up the key by thumbprint.

steps.title: Signature Verified
steps.description: The origin checks the Ed25519 signature over the authority and its freshness; a valid, unexpired signature confirms the agent identity.

steps.title: Spoofed Agent Has No Valid Signature
steps.description: A scraper claiming the same identity via User-Agent cannot produce a valid signature, so verification fails.

steps.title: Policy Decision
steps.description: The origin admits the verified agent, denies unsigned traffic to protected endpoints, and rate-limits or surcharges unverified bots.

name: Inter-Agent Trust & Reputation(IATR)
description: Emerging, mostly draft-stage standards for how an agent prices counterparty risk against an unfamiliar agent without a central gatekeeper. The draft ERC-8004 "Trustless Agents" EIP defines three on-chain registries: Identity (an ERC-721 handle resolving to off-chain agent metadata), Reputation (signed feedback signals), and Validation (validator-contract attestations such as stake-secured re-execution or TEE oracles), deliberately keeping payments and app logic off-chain. A companion trust-model taxonomy classifies mechanisms as brief, claim, proof, stake, reputation, and constraint, arguing no single mechanism suffices and tiered combinations are needed. This is early and unsettled: ERC-8004 is a draft EIP and much of the tooling is nascent. Distinct from authenticated-delegation: that is delegated authority and identity, whereas this is reputational trust priced between economic peers.
features: Identity registry: portable ERC-721 handle resolving to off-chain agent metadata
Reputation registry: signed, aggregatable feedback signals about past behavior
Validation registry: validator attestations (stake-secured re-execution, TEE, zkML)
Trust-model taxonomy: brief, claim, proof, stake, reputation, constraint
Tiered trust proportional to transaction risk, with no central gatekeeper
Payments and application logic kept off-chain by design

tldr.what: Agents price counterparty risk using on-chain identity, reputation, and validator attestations without a central authority, keeping payments and logic off-chain.
tldr.when: Multi-agent systems where unfamiliar agents must transact directly and reputation history is more reliable than centralized vetting.
tldr.watchOut: Standards are draft-stage, tooling is nascent, and reputation gaming or validator collusion can undermine trust signals at scale.

flow.title: Inter-Agent Trust & Reputation
flow.description: Emerging, mostly draft-stage standards (ERC-8004 Identity/Reputation/Validation registries plus a brief/claim/proof/stake/reputation/constraint trust-model taxonomy) for pricing counterparty risk against an unfamiliar agent. Shown here as a buyer agent vetting a seller before transacting, with an escrow fallback. ERC-8004 is a draft EIP and the tooling is early.

Signed feedback signals

✔️ Validation Check

Validator-contract attestations

🚫 Weak Signal
Self-claim alone is insufficient

⚖️ Trust-Model Tiering
brief/claim/proof/stake/reputation/constraint

steps.title: Buyer Finds an Unknown Seller
steps.description: A buyer agent needs a service and discovers an unfamiliar seller agent it has never transacted with.

steps.title: Resolve Identity
steps.description: The buyer resolves the seller handle through the Identity Registry to off-chain AgentFacts and verifies the seller controls that identity.

steps.title: Check Reputation
steps.description: Signed feedback from prior counterparties is aggregated from the Reputation Registry: 340 completed jobs, 2 disputes, recent positive signals.

steps.title: Check Validation Attestations
steps.description: A validator attests via stake-secured re-execution that the seller's last outputs matched spec, recorded in the Validation Registry.

steps.title: Self-Claim Alone Is Insufficient
steps.description: The seller's own claim carries no independent weight; the trust model treats brief or claim signals as too weak for a paid job.

steps.title: Tiered Trust Decision
steps.description: Combining reputation and a validation attestation clears the bar, but because it is the first interaction the buyer requires an escrow fallback.

steps.title: Transact With Escrow, Feed Back Reputation
steps.description: Funds are held in escrow and released on validated delivery; the buyer then submits its own signed feedback, informing future counterparties.
